Human emissions dominate many severe urban smog problems, but vegetation, wildfires, lightning, soils, volcanoes, and other natural sources contribute pollutants and precursors. Misconception: If the sky looks clear, the air is safe. Some important pollutants are invisible at harmful concentrations. Air-quality measurements provide more reliable information than visibility alone. Misconception: Rain permanently solves a smog problem. Rain removes some particles and soluble pollutants, temporarily improving air quality. It does not eliminate the emission sources, so pollution returns when favorable conditions develop again. Frequently Asked Questions What is smog made of? Smog contains varying mixtures of gases and particles. Common components include ozone, nitrogen oxides, sulfur compounds, VOCs, soot, sulfate and nitrate particles, organic aerosols, and other pollutants. What are the two main types of smog? The two traditional types are sulfurous or London-type smog and photochemical or Los Angeles-type smog. What causes photochemical smog? Photochemical smog forms when sunlight drives chemical reactions involving nitrogen oxides, VOCs, and other compounds. Ground-level ozone is one of its most important products. passages.text: What Causes Smog? The main components of photochemical smog, the hazy air pollution that can blanket Los Angeles and other urban areas, are ground-level ozone and particulate matter. What is ozone? Ozone is a greenhouse gas made of three atoms of oxygen. Ozone can be helpful or harmful depending on where it is located. Stratospheric ozone, found in the upper atmosphere (which begins about 5 miles above Earth's surface), forms a protective layer that helps block ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun. Because too much UV exposure can lead to vision loss and skin cancers, the global community began to phase out substances that deplete the stratospheric ozone layer when a hole appeared in 1980. Due to these efforts, the United Nations reports that the layer will likely recover by around 2066. Ground-level ozone, on the other hand, is a pollutant and a primary ingredient of smog. It forms when volatile organic compounds, or VOCs, and nitrogen oxides participate in chemical reactions in the presence of sunlight. - VOCs: Carbon-containing compounds that easily evaporate at room temperature and enter the surrounding air. Tourism and Quality of Life: Areas affected by severe smog often experience reduced tourism, as visitors may be deterred by poor air quality and associated health risks. Smog also impacts the overall quality of life in affected regions, diminishing the attractiveness of cities and hindering outdoor recreational activities. The effects of smog are multifaceted, affecting human health, the environment, and socioeconomic aspects. Tackling smog requires concerted efforts to reduce emissions, improve air quality, and promote sustainable practices. By addressing the causes and consequences of smog, we can strive towards cleaner air, healthier populations, and a more sustainable future. Measuring Smog To understand and address the impact of smog on human health and the environment, accurate measurement and monitoring are essential. The Air Quality Index (AQI) serves as a vital tool in assessing and communicating the level of air pollution, including smog. Both natural and anthropogenic sources produce smog, with airborne particulate matter being a key component. Airborne particulate matter consists of tiny particles and droplets in the air that originate from combustion, industrial processes, and natural sources, playing a significant role in smog formation. To fully comprehend this complex issue, we must explore the various causes that contribute to the formation of smog. Natural Causes Volcanic Activity: Volcanic eruptions release a significant amount of gases, ash, and particulate matter into the atmosphere. These emissions, including sulfur dioxide (SO2) and volcanic ash, can contribute to the formation of smog-like conditions, especially in the vicinity of active volcanoes. Volcanic eruptions can produce smog by releasing pollutants that react in the atmosphere under certain environmental conditions. Forest Fires: Natural forest fires release large quantities of smoke, particulate matter, and gases into the air. The resulting emissions, including carbon monoxide (CO), nitrogen oxides (NOx), and volatile organic compounds (VOCs), can contribute to the formation of smog, particularly in areas affected by widespread wildfires. It is an atmospheric mixture of primary and secondary pollutants. A primary pollutant enters the atmosphere directly from a source. Examples include: - Sulfur dioxide (SO₂) - Nitric oxide (NO) - Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) - Carbon monoxide (CO) - Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) - Soot and other directly emitted particulate matter A secondary pollutant forms in the atmosphere through chemical reactions involving primary pollutants or their reaction products. Examples include: - Ground-level ozone (O₃) - Sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) - Nitric acid (HNO₃) - Sulfate and nitrate particles - Peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN) - Secondary organic aerosols The exact composition of smog varies from place to place and even from hour to hour. Modern usage sometimes treats smog almost synonymously with ground-level ozone pollution, particularly in discussions of summertime urban air quality. However, ozone is more accurately considered an important component of photochemical smog, rather than smog itself. Ground-level ozone is one of its most important products. Why is smog worse on hot, sunny days? Sunlight supplies energy for photochemical reactions, while higher temperatures can accelerate reactions and increase some VOC emissions. Stable, stagnant weather may simultaneously prevent pollutants from dispersing. Why is smog sometimes worse in valleys? Mountains restrict air movement, while temperature inversions can trap polluted air close to the ground. Is smog the same as ozone? No. Ground-level ozone is an important component of photochemical smog, but smog is a mixture containing multiple pollutants. Is smog the same as haze? No. Haze refers to reduced visibility caused largely by tiny suspended particles. Smog can cause haze, but haze can also have other causes. Can smog occur naturally? Some natural events produce smog-like air pollution or contribute strongly to smog formation. Wildfires, volcanic emissions, vegetation, lightning, and soils all release relevant pollutants or precursors. However, severe urban smog is strongly associated with human emissions. This reaction produces ground-level ozone (O3), a key component of photochemical smog. Both natural processes, such as emissions from plants and volcanic activity, and human activities can produce smog through the release of these pollutants. Many VOCs are emitted naturally by plants. Others come from human-made sources, including products such as paints, pesticides, solvents, and processes such as fuel production and combustion. Gas-powered lawn equipment and older-model cars emit particularly high levels of VOCs. Until relatively recently, car emissions were the largest source of VOCs in most cities. However, the catalytic converter almost completely eliminates these emissions in modern vehicles. - Nitrogen oxides: A family of gases that cause pollution and are harmful to human health. Trucks and automobiles are responsible for about half of all nitrogen oxide emissions, with electric power plants and other industrial sources contributing most of the rest. In addition to smog, nitrogen oxides are converted in the atmosphere to nitric acid, a component of acid rain. What is particulate matter? Airborne particulate matter is made up of tiny liquid droplets and solid particles. While some particulate matter is large enough to be visible to the naked eye, much is microscopic. While it may not be possible to eliminate outdoor smog, we can create safer havens indoors by employing effective air purification technologies. Air purifiers equipped with high-quality filters, such as High Efficiency Particulate Air (HEPA) filters and activated carbon filters, are capable of capturing a wide range of pollutants, including fine particulate matter (PM2.5), volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and other harmful gases. By filtering the air, these devices help reduce the concentration of pollutants indoors and create a healthier living environment. It’s important to note that while air purifiers can significantly improve indoor air quality, they should be seen as part of a comprehensive approach to combating smog. Implementing outdoor measures, such as reducing emissions, promoting clean energy sources, and advocating for stricter environmental regulations, remains crucial in addressing the root causes of smog. Photochemical smog is therefore considered to be a problem of modern industrialization. It is present in all modern cities, but it is more common in cities with sunny, warm, dry climates and a large number of motor vehicles.[24] Because it travels with the wind, it can affect sparsely populated areas as well. The composition and chemical reactions involved in photochemical smog were not understood until the 1950s. In 1948, flavor chemist Arie Haagen-Smit adapted some of his equipment to collect chemicals from polluted air, and identified ozone as a component of Los Angeles smog.
